request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 50-year-old Asian woman, was admitted to our hospital due to sudden anterior chest pain. Hematology, biochemistry, and blood gas analyses were performed and found to be normal. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a ground-glass opacity (GGO) in her left S10 lung segment and a solitary small nodule in her left S4 segment. Further testing was carried out, which led to suspicion of lung carcinoma. However, the patient did not provide consent for surgical resection.

After follow-up with CT scans, it was suggested that the GGO was lung carcinoma, and a pathological diagnosis was established through a left lower lobectomy and an upper lung partial resection. The cancer was identified as primary lung adenocarcinoma (localized bronchioloalveolar carcinoma).

There was also a small nodule in her left S4, which was initially suspected to be lung metastasis, however, it was later discovered to be a benign metastasizing leiomyoma (BML). The patient had a history of undergoing a total abdominal hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma in the past, which is why the small nodule was identified as BML.

Management and Outcome:
No additional therapy was given, and the patient was monitored by follow-up chest CT scans over four years. No recurrence of lung cancer or BML could be detected throughout her follow-up.
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Instructions:
The patient is advised to continue her follow-up with her physician and have periodic screening of the chest CT scans.

Scheduled Follow-up Appointments:
Follow-up screening every six months for two years and then annually.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The episode of admitted care that included the lobectomy was for primary lung adenocarcinoma (localized bronchioloalveolar carcinoma). Malignant neoplasm of the bronchus and lung is C34, so the principal diagnosis is C34.

The benign metastasizing leiomyoma (D26/D25-type) was a secondary finding, and the chest pain was only the presenting symptom.

CODE: C34
